person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: CONSPIRACIST IDEATION - the general tendency to engage with conspiracy theories, measured without naming any conspiracy the respondent has to have heard of
span.quote: The psychology of conspiracy theory beliefs is not yet well understood, although research indicates that there are stable individual differences in conspiracist ideation – individuals’ general tendency to engage with conspiracy theories.

span.label: whether a self-report measure can be built from items that carry conspiracist CONTENT but no real-world REFERENT, and what its factor structure is
span.quote: We designed a novel questionnaire consisting of 75 items intended to reflect generic (i.e., non-event-based) conspiracist beliefs. Items were generated by reviewing the academic and popular literature on conspiracy theories. Each item referred to a generic belief which could support belief in various real-world conspiracy theories. To produce generic items, non-specific descriptors such as “certain organizations,” “the government,” and “significant events” were used in place of references to specific entities or events which are the subject of popular conspiracy theories, such as the U.S. government and the 9/11 attacks.

span.label: the 15-item Generic Conspiracist Beliefs scale, drawn from a 75-item pool by exploratory factor analysis into five facets, with reliability and validity evidence across four studies
span.quote: In Study 1, exploratory factor analysis of a novel 75-item measure of non-event-based conspiracist beliefs identified five conspiracist facets. The 15-item GCB scale was developed to sample from each of these themes.

span.label: method
span.quote: In Study 1, exploratory factor analysis of a novel 75-item measure of non-event-based conspiracist beliefs identified five conspiracist facets. The 15-item GCB scale was developed to sample from each of these themes.

span.label: a MONOLOGICAL BELIEF SYSTEM - specific conspiracy beliefs supported by a small set of generic convictions about how the world works, such as that governments routinely harm and deceive their citizens
span.quote: This is consistent with the idea that conspiracist ideation is a monological belief system (Goertzel, 1994 ; Wood et al., 2012 ) in which beliefs in many individual conspiracy theories are supported by relatively generic convictions such as the belief that governments routinely harm and deceive their citizens.

span.label: 75 generic items written by replacing every specific entity and event with a non-specific descriptor, factor-analysed on 489 self-selected online respondents, then reduced to 15 sampling each facet and validated across three further studies

span.label: THE INSTRUMENT'S DESIGN IS A SUBSTITUTION RULE: `non-specific descriptors such as CERTAIN ORGANIZATIONS, THE GOVERNMENT, and SIGNIFICANT EVENTS were used IN PLACE OF references to specific entities or events`. What makes an item generic is a lexical operation on its noun phrases
span.quote: We designed a novel questionnaire consisting of 75 items intended to reflect generic (i.e., non-event-based) conspiracist beliefs. Items were generated by reviewing the academic and popular literature on conspiracy theories. Each item referred to a generic belief which could support belief in various real-world conspiracy theories. To produce generic items, non-specific descriptors such as “certain organizations,” “the government,” and “significant events” were used in place of references to specific entities or events which are the subject of popular conspiracy theories, such as the U.S. government and the 9/11 attacks.

span.label: and the theoretical claim that licenses it: conspiracist ideation is `A MONOLOGICAL BELIEF SYSTEM in which beliefs in many individual conspiracy theories are supported by relatively generic convictions such as the belief that GOVERNMENTS ROUTINELY HARM AND DECEIVE THEIR CITIZENS`
span.quote: This is consistent with the idea that conspiracist ideation is a monological belief system (Goertzel, 1994 ; Wood et al., 2012 ) in which beliefs in many individual conspiracy theories are supported by relatively generic convictions such as the belief that governments routinely harm and deceive their citizens.

span.label: THE FACTOR STRUCTURE THAT DEFINES THE INSTRUMENT COMES FROM A SELF-SELECTED ONLINE SAMPLE recruited by `a BLOG POST ON PSYCHOLOGYTODAY.COM and a public PSYCHOLOGY OF THE PARANORMAL EMAILING LIST`, with `no reward offered`. The five facets are a property of who answered that call
span.quote: To recruit a large and diverse sample not composed exclusively of undergraduate psychology students, volunteers were requested via a blog post on psychologytoday.com and a public “Psychology of the Paranormal” emailing list. In all, 500 participants (225 females, 269 males; no gender data for 6 respondents) completed the questionnaire. Data from 11 participants missing data for 2 or more items were omitted (total valid N = 489). Age ranged from 18 to 87 years ( M = 35.9; SD = 13.9). The majority of participants indicated that they were British (43.8%) or American (26.4%). Other nationalities accounted for 25.6% of the sample (4.2% did not provide nationality information). No reward was offered for taking part. Self-selected respondents completed the questionnaire online via a web-based interface.

span.label: the five facets may not be five things: they `WERE HIGHLY INTERCORRELATED`, and the paper allows that they may themselves be `a product of EVEN MORE ABSTRACT IDEAS, SUCH AS AN ESSENTIAL DISTRUST OF AUTHORITY`. The dimensionality is a choice about where to stop
span.quote: Given the intercorrelations between the five conspiracist facets observed here, it is feasible that these convictions are themselves a product of even more abstract ideas, such as an essential distrust of authority.

span.label: and the paper's verdict on its own instrument is MARKED AS AN OPINION, which is rarer than it should be: `IT IS OUR OPINION that the most successful measure ... will be one which achieves an appropriate balance between specificity and abstractness, AS WE FEEL WE HAVE ACHIEVED with the GCB`
span.quote: While it may be possible to construct a measure which aims to tap into these abstract sentiments, it is our opinion that the most successful measure of conspiracist ideation will be one which achieves an appropriate balance between specificity and abstractness, as we feel we have achieved with the GCB.

span.label: THE COMPARISON WITH THE COMPETING INSTRUMENT WAS NEVER RUN: `Both approaches may have advantages and limitations in certain contexts ... FUTURE RESEARCH MAY SEEK TO COMPARE measures of conspiracist ideation across different cultures DIRECTLY`. Two scales, one construct, one journal, one year, and no head-to-head
span.quote: Both approaches may have advantages and limitations in certain contexts. The relatively more generic approach of the CMQ may have particular advantages when studying non-Western and non-democratic cultures. Future research may seek to compare measures of conspiracist ideation across different cultures directly.

span.label: the definition the introduction runs on is QUOTED FROM A TRADE BOOK: `a conspiracist belief can be described as THE UNNECESSARY ASSUMPTION OF CONSPIRACY WHEN OTHER EXPLANATIONS ARE MORE PROBABLE (Aaronovitch, 2009, p. 5)`. It carries a normative judgement - `unnecessary`, `more probable` - into a psychometric paper
span.quote: A conspiracist belief can be described as “the unnecessary assumption of conspiracy when other explanations are more probable

span.label: discriminant validity against theoretically unrelated constructs - sensation-seeking, emotional intelligence and the Big Five - in a separate general-public sample
span.note: eliminates: the objection that the scale measures a general personality factor rather than conspiracist ideation · outcome: held

span.label: GCB
span.quote: The GCB specifies the content and objectives of some conspiracies (e.g., the suppression of new technology) while remaining non-specific about any entities or events involved in the conspiracies. In contrast, Bruder et al.’s Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ) remains largely non-specific in regards to both objectives and entities or events, with the exception of referring to specifically political conspiracies.

span.note: WHOSE RESULT THIS IS: other research which has found - 2026-08-26 terminal-a. THE SUBJECT OF THIS RESULT IS AN INDEFINITE STUDY, NOT THIS PAPER. `Previous studies reported`, `studies in guinea pig showed`, `recent studies have reported` - somebody else's work under a common noun rather than a name, with a citation in the sentence and no first-person marker. The quote is verbatim and the claim is true; only the attribution is wrong. FOUND BY MEASURING MY OWN CUE'S RECALL: the first sweep required a NAMED author as the subject (`Sperling (1960) demonstrated`) and found 17. Reading eleven citation-bearing findings on `Plakke2016` by hand showed four the cue could not see - `A study examining recognition found`, `studies of typical human subjects have demonstrated`, `A follow up study found` - so the named cue's 17 was a floor and not a count. A CUE'S FALSE POSITIVES TELL YOU NOTHING ABOUT ITS FALSE NEGATIVES, and the only way to find these was to read a record's whole layer. Q-1118.
